title: Facing Islamophobia
hookLine: prejudice against Muslims, and how communities respond with patience and openness

cards: A note taped to a mosque door overnight. Ugly words, misspelled, telling the people inside to go home, when this is home. The imam finds it before dawn prayer.
What happens next is a choice. Some mosques that have faced moments like this have answered by opening the doors wider: an open day, tea in the hall, a sign that says come in and ask us anything.
It isn't the only answer, and it isn't easy.

teach.b: Islamophobia is the word people use for prejudice and hostility toward Muslims, and toward people taken to be Muslim because of a name, a beard or a headscarf.
It can be a shout on a bus, a vandalized wall, or a door that quietly stays closed at a job interview. The tradition has its own memory of rejection.
In Sahih al-Bukhari, 'A'ishah asks the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, whether he ever had a day harder than the battle of Uhud.
He says yes: a day he went to a man of standing to ask for support, and was turned away. He walked off so grieved, he says, that he hardly knew where he was until he reached a place on the road.
Then an angel of the mountains came and offered to bring the two mountains down on the town. And he said no. He hoped, instead, that from their descendants would come people who worship God alone.

teach.h: REPEL THE EVIL DEED WITH A BETTER ONE.
teach.b: The Qur'an puts the principle in Surah Fussilat, in Pickthall: "Repel the evil deed with one which is better." The one who was your enemy, it goes on, may become like a close friend.
In Surah al-Furqan, the servants of the Merciful answer the ignorant who address them with: peace.
But patience isn't the same as silence. Communities also document what happens, report it, and turn to the law. The Prophet's answer that day wasn't to pretend nothing had happened.
It was to refuse to answer in kind, and keep a future open.

how: Muslim communities facing prejudice respond in different ways: some mosques hold open days and invite neighbors in, while community groups also document incidents, support those targeted, and work with the police and the courts.

o: meeting prejudice against Muslims with patience, not in kind
a fear of Islam that only Muslims themselves can feel
staying silent about hate so as not to make it worse

p: repel the evil deed with a better one
when the ignorant address them: peace
no: he hoped for their descendants

s: Islamophobia only affects people who are Muslim
it can fall on anyone taken to be Muslim because of a name, a beard or a headscarf.
in the report in al-Bukhari, the Prophet calls this day harder than the battle of Uhud
'A'ishah asked, and he told her about the day he was turned away.
answering with patience means saying nothing and reporting nothing
patience isn't silence: communities also document, report, and turn to the law.

games.q: you've just been turned away by a town's leaders, and you're grieving on the road. an angel offers to bring the mountains down on them. what do you say?
o: no: I hope their descendants will worship God.
wait and see what they do next.
games.why: he refused, hoping that from their descendants would come people who worship God alone. the town that turned him away is spared.

practice: Picture a train, a store, a sidewalk, where someone is being shouted at for how they look or pray.
You don't confront the shouter: you walk over, stand beside the person targeted, say something ordinary, hi, are you okay, want to walk with me, and stay until it's over, then ask what they need.
If you pray, hold that person in mind; if you don't, rehearse that first sentence until it's yours.

wordCard.voice: Facing Islamophobia. Prejudice against Muslims, met with patience, openness, and the refusal to answer in kind. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: patience, steadfastness: holding firm without answering in kind.

carryVoice: Your line: answer hate with good. Patience, and a future kept open. That's today, done.
